highlights.text: setting out or departing from one place to another (al-shukhūṣ)
ẓaʿana / yaẓʿanu (verbal nouns: ẓaʿn, ẓaʿan) = 'to depart, set out, move on, journey.'
whose flanks wear through every ẓiʿān (binding-rope)
Freshness, or a thing being before its proper/due time (not yet ripe/settled).
Stillness — a thing standing still with little movement.
one core root meaning the passing-on of something and the moving-along within something
Go crosswise along the tracks and range about, as Orion goes crosswise among the stars.
the root's core sense is heaviness and severity/intensity
Tafnīd — blame or censure.
he specifies it only applies when the old age comes with a decline of the mind — not old age alone
a single sound root whose core meaning is trial and testing (ibtilāʾ, ikhtibār)
A concrete example is fatantu al-dhahaba bi'l-nār, "I assayed the gold with fire," i.e. tested it.
If she has beguiled me, yesterday she beguiled Saʿīd…
as producing two opposite meanings: (1) deliverance/escape, and (2) destruction/dying
فَازَ / يَفُوزُ (fāza/yafūzu): to escape safely, be delivered; the agent noun is fāʾiz.
on divorcing his wife a man would say فُوزِي بِأَمْرِكِ ("take charge of your own affair")
**غصب (ghaṣb)** — one sense: taking something wrongfully and by force/coercion.
the milla, the creed/religious community that the Muslims adhere to as their religion
highlights.note: the book's own gloss of Q 2:138

highlights.text: around one core idea — السَّتْر (covering, concealing)
غَفَرَ اللَّهُ ذَنْبَهُ, "God covered/forgave his sin"
An Arab woman told her daughter اغْفِرِي غَفِيرَكِ — "cover it."
uprightness/standing erect.
illustrated with a line of poetry about a singer poised upright while performing
A hadith is cited: "the likeness of the hypocrite is like the cedar standing fixed on the ground, until its uprooting comes all at once" — al-mujdhiyah glossed as "the firmly-standing one."
gathering and drawing something together/inward.
the earth is called a كِفَات, "a gatherer," "of the living and of the dead."
Poetic shāhid from Ru'ba — a fragmentary line using كَفْت in this same gathering/binding sense, likened to a fire's blaze.
kilā is to the dual what kull ("all") is to the plural.
He also cites kiltā l-jannatayni ātat ukulahā ("each of the two gardens yielded its produce", Q 18:33).
a single sound root whose core sense is interpenetration — parts entering into and interlocking with one another
Flesh / meat (اللحم): the base sense from which the root's image is drawn.
a gladness so intense that one can hardly stay still — exuberant, restless delight (ṭarab)
Qur'anic citation (40:75): "wa-bi-mā kuntum tamraḥūn" — "and for your exultant/insolent gladness."
an aging man asks whether his grey hair now bars him from his mirāḥ
one core idea: one thing coming apart from another, being set apart or held distinct
يَكَادُ يَتَمَيَّزُ غَيْظًا, "he almost comes apart with rage."
until the skin of its head came away (انْمَازَ) from the bone
Al-na'y — distance, remoteness.
a verse contrasting how a person treats you when rich versus poor — friendly ("softens his side") when you're wealthy, but "turns away [nā'a] and grows estranged" when you're poor
all of whose branches trace back to one core sense: to contemplate and behold a thing
نَظَرْتُ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ ("I looked at the thing") = you beheld it.
a line of verse: "if you two wait for me a single night… it will profit me at Umm Jundab's."
one root whose single idea is strength.
The rukn of a thing is its strongest side.
رَكَنَ إِلَيْهِ — "to incline toward / rely on."
he takes shelter at a strong rukn," i.e. at might and protection that cannot be breached
most uses of this root trace to two core ideas: heedlessness/inattention (ghaflah) and stillness (sukūn)
The base verb sahawtu means "I was heedless/inattentive"
the phrase jā'a sahwan rahwan, "he came calmly, unhurriedly."
al-salkh is stripping the skin off an animal, i.e. flaying.
a month is said to "salakha" or "insalakha," i.e. to pass/slip away, as though it were being stripped off like a skin.
"naslakhu minhu al-nahar" — "We strip the day away from it [the night],"
a single core idea: giving a thing water — or the like — to drink.
سَقَى / أَسْقَى = "to give (someone) drink" or "to appoint someone a supply of water."
cited from Ibn Aḥmar: "nor do I 'water my waterskin' against any whom I have opposed."
al-sāḥah is a wide, open place, and the courtyard of a house (sāḥat al-dār) is named from it.
Q 37:177: "and when it comes down into their courtyard".
Al-Rāghib glosses al-sāʾiḥūn (Q 9:112) as al-ṣāʾimūn, "those who fast"

fasting is of two kinds: fasting by legal ruling, which is abstaining from food and sexual relations, and real fasting, which is guarding the bodily organs (hearing, sight, tongue) from acts of disobedience
the falling and occurrence of a thing, from which further senses branch.
"fa-idhā wajabat junūbuhā" — "then when their flanks fall [to the ground]" — i.e. once they have died
a line of poetry by Qays about a tribe's "first casualty."
A hadith uses this verb for death itself: "once he has wajaba, let no wailing woman weep."
several origins that, in his judgement, are very sharply distinct from one another
is to appraise by guesswork how much fruit they will bear
Ibn Fāris derives al-kharrāṣ, "the liar," from this sense: such a person says what he does not know and cannot establish as true.
one root meaning: agitation and falling, accompanied by a sound.
kharra means "he fell."
Ibn Fāris cites Abū Khirāsh describing a sword: "With it I leave the armed warrior upon his hands, falling; you would take him for a qashīb vulture."
one root meaning hiddenness and a sinking or caving inward.
khasf / khasaf is the caving-in of the earth's surface. His Qur'anic citation is 28:81, "So We caused the earth to swallow him and his dwelling."
He cites a verse: "a copious [well], of the deep khusuf wells."
